query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Annealed pure copper exhibits enhanced ductility compared to its as-fabricated state because its face‐centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure, when freed from residual stresses by annealing, permits the activation of multiple slip systems during deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated pure copper with inherent residual stresses and non-equiaxed grain structure.
generation.intervention: Thermal annealing to relieve residual stresses and refine the grain structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading under controlled laboratory conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure with numerous slip systems.
generation.mechanism: Annealing reduces dislocation pile-ups and promotes equiaxed grain formation, thereby enhancing the activation of multiple slip systems which facilitate plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed pure copper samples will show a significantly higher elongation at fracture (improved ductility) compared to their non-annealed counterparts during tensile tests.
generation.baseline: Non-annealed pure copper samples expected to have lower ductility due to higher residual stresses and less optimal grain structures.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated for high-purity, minimally alloyed copper; presence of significant impurities or alternate crystallographic defects could moderate the ductility improvement.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement in ductility may vary with annealing temperature, time, and initial microstructural conditions. Effects of minor impurities or variations in grain size on ductility are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of pure copper samples: one set subjected to a standardized annealing process and one left in the as-fabricated condition. Conduct standard tensile tests at room temperature on both sets.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed copper samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (i.e., percentage elongation) compared to as-fabricated samples, or if an unexpected reduction in ductility is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
